metadata.scope: e_france (de jure Empire of Francia in skachano/tarraconian_hre)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic (post-867 foundation, post-867 eponym, post-867 Norman/Old Norse coinage, or post-867 renaming).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty who lived after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier) that can serve as an alternative historical base for Tarraconian. Excludes reconstructed (*starred) forms and names only attested after 867. Includes exists (bool), names (list), first_mention_year (int <= 867), first_mention_source, relationship, and notes.

b_quimper.first_mention_attestation: 1084–1112 (Kemper / Apud Kemper Conrentini; earlier Roman Aquilonia)

natural_proper_name.name: Confluence of the Odet and Steïr rivers

b_quimper.etymology_analysis: From Breton 'kemper' ('confluence', Celtic *kom-bero-), referring to the confluence of the Odet and Steïr rivers. First attested in charters as Kemper (1084–1112; Latinized Confluentia 1166), succeeding Roman Aquilonia; the Breton topographic name and episcopal seat of Saint Corentin (5th–6th c.) predate 867. Not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman/late-antique name of the Locmaria settlement (Aquilonia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Aquilonia preceded Breton Kemper ('confluence').

morphemes.translation: East / Orient (after the ship Soleil d'Orient)

b_lorient.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1666 as a shipyard of the French East India Company; first attested as Lorient in 1670, contracted from 'L'Orient' after the first ship built there, Soleil d'Orient (1667–1671). Completely anachronistic for 867. Not named after a person or natural proper name.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Archembaldstat — Municipal foundation chartered by Archembald
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (1666 French East India Company port); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Archembald of House Kestenholz-Sitzichow.

b_cornouailles.first_mention_attestation: 9th century (Cornugallia / Cornubia in Vita Sancti Samsonis and Cartulary of Landévennec)

morphemes.translation: horn, peninsula, or tribe of the Cornovii

b_cornouailles.etymology_analysis: Breton Kernev, Latin Cornugallia / Cornubia, attested in the early Middle Ages (9th c. lives of Saints Samson and Winwaloe), derived from the Brittonic tribal name Cornovii (from Celtic *kornu-, 'horn/peninsula', transferred from British Cornwall). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person or hydronym.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Archembaldszelle — Disambiguated foundation: Monastic cell endowed by Archembald of House Sitzichow
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated sub-barony foundation.

natural_proper_name.name: Promontory / hill above the Penfeld estuary

b_brest.etymology_analysis: First attested as Bresta in 856 (predating 867; also site of a late Roman castellum). Likely from a Celtic/Breton root *bre- / *brist- denoting a hill or elevated promontory overlooking the Penfeld. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Zant-Pôl-van-Lejôn).

b_st_pol_de_leon.first_mention_attestation: c. 869–870 (Oppidum Pauli / Sancti Paulinanni Leonini Fanum; 884 Vita Pauli Aureliani)
b_st_pol_de_leon.eponym_details: Named after Saint Paul Aurelian (6th-century Breton bishop, pre-867)
b_st_pol_de_leon.etymology_analysis: Attested c. 869–870 as Oppidum Pauli / Sancti Paulinanni Leonini Fanum, named after the 6th-century founding bishop Saint Paul Aurelian (pre-867) and the regional name Léon (from Latin legio, 'legion', referring to a Roman garrison). Historical for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Zant-Pol de Lôn (constituent holding of Zant-Pôl-van-Lejôn)

b_nantes.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Ptolemy: Condevincum; 4th c. Civitas Namnetum / Namnetes)

morphemes.translation: valley dwellers / Gaulish tribe of the Namnetes

b_nantes.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Condevincum (2nd c. AD, Ptolemy), replaced in Late Antiquity (4th c.) by the ethnonym Namnetes (from Celtic *nanto-, 'valley' or 'stream'), giving modern Nantes (Breton Naoned). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geography (2nd c. AD, Kondēoúinkon)
older_name_by_867.notes: Condevincum was the original Gaulish name before the ethnonym Namnetes (> Nantes) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

b_rais.first_mention_attestation: 9th century (pagus Ratiatensis / Radesius; from Roman Ratiatum, 2nd c. AD)

morphemes.translation: fortress / rampart (or fern-place), Roman port of Rezé

b_rais.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Carolingian pagus Ratiatensis / Radesius (9th c.), itself named after the Gallo-Roman port city of Ratiatum (modern Rezé, from Gaulish *ratis, 'rampart/fortress' or 'fern'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

morphemes.translation: part, share, or parcel of land

b_guerande.etymology_analysis: First attested in 854 as Werran (9th c. Uuenrann), from Old Breton gwen ('white/blessed', possibly referencing salt pans) + rann ('parcel/territory'). Clearly historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_chateaubriant.eponym_details: Named after Brient (11th-century Breton baron who built the castle c. 1015–1050)
b_chateaubriant.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 11th century as Castellum Brienti, combining French château (< Latin castellum, 'castle') with the Breton personal name Brient, the 11th-century lord who founded the fortress near the older parish of Béré. Anachronistic for 867 because it is named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient 9th-century Breton parish and priory of Béré on the Chère (in-game: Bêrê)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 Breton parish restored over 1050 motte castle of Brient.

b_saint_brieuc.first_mention_attestation: 1032 (Sanctus Briocus; monastery founded by St. Brioc in the 6th c.)
b_saint_brieuc.eponym_details: Named after Saint Brioc (c. 409–c. 502, 5th–6th c. Welsh/Breton saint, pre-867)
b_saint_brieuc.etymology_analysis: First attested in surviving charters as Sanctus Briocus in 1032, though the monastery and bishopric honor Saint Brioc (5th–6th c., pre-867) and the see was established by Nominoë in 848. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_treguier.first_mention_attestation: c. 1050 (monasterium Sancti Tutuali Pabut; Lantreguer 1267, from regional Trecor 9th c.)

natural_proper_name.name: Trégor (Breton Treger, land of the three tribes/pagi)

b_treguier.etymology_analysis: Originally called Saint-Pabu / Monasterium Sancti Tutuali (c. 1050, after 6th-c. St. Tudwal); the form Lantreguer / Tréguier ('monastery of Trégor', from Breton lann + Treger < *tri-corio-, 'three armies') only appears from 1267. While the diocese of Trégor dates to the 9th c., the town name Tréguier is post-867.

b_saint_malo.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (episcopal seat transferred from Alet to Insula Aaronis / Saint-Malo in 1146; St. Malo lived 6th–7th c.)
b_saint_malo.eponym_details: Named after Saint Malo / Maclovius (c. 520–621, pre-867), though the island was called Insula Aaronis in 867
b_saint_malo.etymology_analysis: Named after the 6th–7th c. bishop Saint Malo (pre-867). However, in 867 the episcopal city was Alet (Aleth) and the rock itself was called Insula Aaronis ('Island of Aaron'); Saint-Malo only became the town and bishopric name in the 12th century (1146). Anachronistic as a city title for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400 AD, Aletum); 6th-c. Insula Aaronis
older_name_by_867.notes: Until 1146 the episcopal city was Alet (attested c. 400), while the rock of Saint-Malo itself was called Insula Aaronis (6th c.).

b_rennes.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Condate; 4th c. Civitas Riedonum / Redones)

morphemes.translation: chariot-drivers / riders (Gaulish tribe of the Riedones)

b_rennes.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Condate ('confluence', of the Ille and Vilaine), replaced in the 4th century by the tribal name Riedones (from Celtic *rēd-, 'to ride/drive chariots'), evolving into Rennes. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy and Peutinger Table (2nd–4th c. AD, Condate)
older_name_by_867.notes: Condate ('confluence') was the original Gaulish name before Riedones (> Rennes) replaced it in the 4th c.

morphemes.translation: stream or fortified town (later reinterpreted as French bourg)

b_combourg.etymology_analysis: First attested 1030–1066 as Comburn (later Combor, Combourg), associated with the castle built in the early 11th century (1016–1040) by Archbishop Junkeneus of Dol. Post-867 feudal foundation with no pre-867 attestation; anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Umarszelle — Monastic cell endowed by Umar of House QasiLippe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (1014-1040 castle built by Archbishop of Dol); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Umar of House Qasi-Lippe.

b_vannes.first_mention_attestation: 56 BC (Veneti in Caesar; 2nd c. AD Darioritum; 4th c. Civitas Venetum)

morphemes.translation: friendly ones / kinsmen (Gaulish tribe of the Veneti)

b_vannes.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Darioritum, replaced in Late Antiquity (4th–5th c.) by the ethnonym of the Gaulish Veneti (attested since Julius Caesar, 56 BC), yielding Vannes (Breton Gwened). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy and Peutinger Table (2nd–4th c. AD, Darioritum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Darioritum was the Roman name before Veneti (> Vannes) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

natural_proper_name.name: Forest of Brocéliande / central Breton forest ('land across the forest')

b_porhoet.etymology_analysis: First attested in 833 as Poutrecoet (glossed in 868 as pagus trans sylvam, 'country beyond the forest'), from Old Breton pou (< Latin pagus) + tre ('beyond') + coet ('forest'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_rohan.first_mention_attestation: 11th–12th century (Rohan 1127; castle founded c. 1120 by Alain I of Rohan)
b_rohan.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 11th century / 1127 as Rohan, a Breton oronym from roc'h ('rock') + diminutive -an ('little rock'). Although based on a natural feature, the town and castle were founded in the early 12th century (c. 1120–1128) by Alain I of Porhoët/Rohan, making the barony title anachronistic for 867.

b_angers.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Ptolemy: Juliomagus; 4th c. Civitas Andecavorum / Andecavi)

morphemes.translation: intensive prefix + 'hollow/cavity' or 'heroes' (Gaulish tribe of the Andecavi)

b_angers.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Juliomagus (2nd c. AD), replaced in Late Antiquity by the ethnonym of the Gaulish Andecavi (attested since Caesar), yielding Angers. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy (2nd c. AD) and Peutinger Table (Iuliomago)
older_name_by_867.notes: Juliomagus was the Roman name before Andecavi (> Angers) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

b_luigne.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1186 as Lugniacum when the parish was carved out of Tarençay by Bishop Raoul of Beaumont. While the formation uses the Gallo-Roman estate suffix -acum, the settlement and parish are unattested before 1186; anachronistic as a barony title for 867.

morphemes.translation: cleft, boundary post, or arrow (folk-etymologized as 'arrow')

b_la_fleche.etymology_analysis: First attested 1060–1081 as Feza / Fecia and 1087 Fissa (from Latin fissa, 'split/cleft' or fixia, 'fixed boundary', later reshaped to French flèche, 'arrow'). Grew around an 11th-century castle built by Jean de Beaugency; anachronistic for 867.

b_le_lude.first_mention_attestation: 976 (Lusedus, in a charter of Geoffrey Grisegonelle, Count of Anjou)

morphemes.translation: clearing / bright open place (or Gaulish personal/topographic stem)

b_le_lude.etymology_analysis: First attested in 976 as Lusedus in a charter of Geoffrey Grisegonelle, Count of Anjou (linked to Latin lucius, 'bright/clearing', or a Gallo-Roman fortress built to defend Anjou against Viking raids in the late 9th–10th c.). Unattested before 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_craon.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Cravio in Gregory of Tours; 847 refuge of Count Lambert of Nantes)
b_craon.etymology_analysis: First attested as Cravio by Gregory of Tours in the 6th century (later Credonium) and recorded in 847 during the Frankish-Breton wars. Derived from a pre-Celtic/Gaulish root *crav- ('stone/rock'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_le_mans.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Ptolemy: Vindinum; 4th c. Civitas Cenomanorum)

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Aulerci Cenomani (yielding Mans / Maine)

b_le_mans.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Vindinon / Vindunum ('white fortress/place', 2nd c. AD), replaced in Late Antiquity by the ethnonym of the Gaulish Cenomani, evolving via Celmans to Le Mans. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geography (2nd c. AD, Vindinon / Vindunum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Vindinum ('white hillfort') was the original Gaulish name before Cenomani (> Le Mans) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

b_courcillon.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 11th century (Cuercelone) as the seat of the medieval feudal family of Courcillon, likely a diminutive of Late Latin curticella ('small manor/estate'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_sarthe.first_mention_attestation: Early Middle Ages (Latin Sarta; river name Sarthe)
b_sarthe.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Sarthe River (Latin Sarta), an ancient pre-Celtic/Indo-European hydronym from *ser-/*sar- ('to flow'). As an ancient river name, the stem is historical for 867 (note: current repo maps b_sarthe to Ballon).

b_sable.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th / 11th century (Sabolium / Sobloilum; medieval fortress on the Sarthe)
b_sable.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Latin charters from the late 10th–11th century as Sabolium / Sobloilum, from Latin sabulum ('sand') referencing local red sand quarries, growing around a medieval border fortress between Maine and Anjou. Unattested before 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_mayenne.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Meduana; Carolingian stronghold on the Mayenne River)

morphemes.translation: to burst forth, be wet, overflow

b_mayenne.etymology_analysis: Attested as Meduana from the 6th century (later Medena, Maesne 1265), named after the Mayenne River—a Gaulish hydronym from *mad- ('wet/overflowing') + -uenna. Also a Carolingian border stronghold; historical for 867.

b_laval.first_mention_attestation: c. 1020 (Vallis Guidonis; town founded in the 11th century by Guy I of Laval)
b_laval.etymology_analysis: Did not exist before the 11th century; founded c. 1020 around a rocky promontory castle by Guy I of Laval (Vallis Guidonis). From Old French la val ('the valley', Latin vallis). Clearly anachronistic for 867.

b_saumur.etymology_analysis: First attested in 968 as Salmuri (later castrum Salmurum), growing around the 10th-century fortress of Theobald the Trickster of Blois. Etymology is uncertain (possibly pre-Celtic *sala 'marsh' or Latin salvus murus 'safe wall'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

morphemes.translation: personal name Mellius (or Latin maletum 'apple orchard')

b_melay.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1019 as Melei (either Gallo-Roman *Melliacum or Latin maletum 'apple orchard'). No pre-867 attestation exists; anachronistic as a barony title for 867.

b_angouleme.first_mention_attestation: c. 380–390 (Iculisma in Ausonius; c. 400 civitas Ecolismensium; 511 Ecolisina)
b_angouleme.etymology_analysis: First attested c. 380–390 by the poet Ausonius as Iculisma (civitas Ecolismensium c. 400, Engolisma in the Middle Ages). An ancient pre-Roman/Gaulish toponym of obscure root. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_saint_junien.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (hermitage and tomb of Saint Junian, d. 540; collegiate church attested 10th–11th c.)
b_saint_junien.eponym_details: Named after Saint Junian of Limousin (d. 540 AD, pre-867)
b_saint_junien.etymology_analysis: Named after Saint Junian (Latin Junianus), a 6th-century Limousin hermit (d. 540) around whose tomb a monastery and settlement developed at the earlier site of Comodoliac. Because the eponymous saint and cult predate 867, the name is historical for 867.

b_cognac.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1075–1101 as Comniaco (Conniaco c. 1080), from the Gallo-Roman personal name Connius + Gaulish suffix -acum ('estate of Connius'). Although the toponymic formation is Gallo-Roman in type, the town and castle are unattested before the late 10th–11th century; flagged anachronistic under the 867 attestation threshold.

b_la_rochelle.first_mention_attestation: 961 (Rupella; chartered as a port city in the 12th c. by William X of Aquitaine)

natural_proper_name.name: Small rocky promontory amidst coastal marshes

b_la_rochelle.etymology_analysis: First attested in 961 as Rupella (French La Rochelle, 'the little rock', from *rocca + diminutive -elle), referring to a rocky promontory in the marshes near the older hamlet of Cougnes; developed as a port only in the 12th century after the decline of Châtelaillon. Anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_taillebourg.first_mention_attestation: 1267 (Terra Talleburgi; fortress built in the 10th–11th century)
b_taillebourg.etymology_analysis: First attested as Terra Talleburgi in 1267 (fortress erected in the 10th–11th c. overlooking the Charente). A characteristic high-medieval French compound of taille- (from tailler, 'cut/clear') + bourg ('fortified town'). Clearly anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Christinestat — Municipal foundation chartered by Christine
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (10th-11th century Charente fortress); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Christine under Toponym-First foundation (disqualifying circular in-game house).

b_limoges.first_mention_attestation: c. 10 BC (Augustoritum; 4th c. Civitas Lemovicum / Lemovicas)

morphemes.translation: fighters, victors ('elm-fighters', tribe of the Lemovices)

b_limoges.etymology_analysis: Founded c. 10 BC as Roman Augustoritum ('ford of Augustus'), replaced from the 4th century by Lemovicas from the Gaulish tribe Lemovices (lemo- 'elm' + -vices 'fighters/victors'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman foundation (c. 10 BC), Ptolemy & Peutinger Table (Augustoritum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Augustoritum ('ford of Augustus') was the Roman name before Lemovices (> Limoges) replaced it in the 4th c.

b_chalus.first_mention_attestation: 8th–9th century (Vita Brevior of St. Vaast: Leucus / Castrum Leucus; later Castel Lucius)
b_chalus.etymology_analysis: Occitan Chasluç, from Castrum Leucus / Castel Lucius ('fortress of Lucius' or Gaulish *leuco- 'bright'), linked to the 8th–9th century Vita Brevior of Saint Vaast (who was born at Leucus). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_ventadour.first_mention_attestation: c. 1060 (castle built by Ebles I of Ventadour; viscounty created in the 11th c.)

natural_proper_name.name: Windy rocky spur above the Soudeillette

b_ventadour.etymology_analysis: From Occitan Ventadorn (Latin ventatorium, 'windy place'), referring to the exposed rocky spur in Corrèze. The castle and viscounty of Ventadour were founded in the mid-11th century (c. 1060) by Ebles I of Comborn; anachronistic as a barony title for 867.

b_turenne.first_mention_attestation: 767 (castrum of Turenne captured by Pepin the Short; 823 viscounts of Turenne)
b_turenne.etymology_analysis: First attested in 767 when the castrum of Turenne was taken by Pepin the Short (with vicaria Torinensis and viscounts recorded in 823). Derived from a pre-Celtic oronymic root *tur- ('height/hill') + -enna. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_perigueux.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Petrocorii in Caesar; Roman Vesunna; 4th c. Civitas Petrocoriorum)

morphemes.translation: armies, clans ('four clans/armies', tribe of the Petrocorii)

b_perigueux.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Vesunna, replaced in Late Antiquity by the Gaulish tribal name Petrocorii (attested since Caesar, 52 BC; from Gaulish petro- 'four' + -corii 'clans/armies'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy & Peutinger Table (2nd–4th c. AD, Vesunna)
older_name_by_867.notes: Vesunna was the Roman name before Petrocorii (> Périgueux) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

b_nontron.first_mention_attestation: 8th century (Nantron / Natadum; abbey donated to Charroux Abbey c. 785)
b_nontron.etymology_analysis: Occitan Nontron, attested from the late 8th century (c. 785, donation to Charroux Abbey). Derived either from the Gallo-Roman personal name Nantironius or from Gaulish *nanto- ('valley'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_montignac.first_mention_attestation: 11th century (Montignacum; medieval castle of the Counts of Périgord)

morphemes.translation: personal name Montanius (from montanus 'of the mountain')

b_montignac.etymology_analysis: First attested as Montignacum in the 11th century, from the widespread Gallo-Roman type *Montaniacum (Latin Montanius + Gaulish -acum). Despite the Gallo-Roman suffix pattern, the settlement is unattested before the 11th century; flagged anachronistic under strict 867 attestation.

b_bergerac.first_mention_attestation: 1100 (Brageyrack; castle established in the late 11th century)
b_bergerac.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1100 as Brageyrack (later Brageyrac), from the Gallo-Roman personal/occupational name Bracarius (Gaulish braca 'breeches') + -acum ('estate of Bracarius'). Although the stem is Gallo-Roman, the town grew around an 11th-century fortress and has no pre-867 attestation.

b_saintonge.first_mention_attestation: 58 BC (Santones in Caesar; Late Latin Santonica / pagus Santonicus)

morphemes.translation: territorial adjective suffix ('land of the Santones')

b_saintonge.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin Santonica ('territory of the Santones'), derived from the Gaulish tribe Santones attested since Julius Caesar (58 BC). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_jonzac.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Latin as Joenzacus / Joviniacum from the 11th century, from a Gallo-Roman personal name (Juventius or Jucundus) + -acum ('estate of'). Although rooted in a Gallo-Roman villa site, no pre-867 textual attestation of the name survives.

b_royan.first_mention_attestation: 11th century (Roiannum / Roianum / Rugiano in the foundation charter of Saint-Nicolas priory)
b_royan.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 11th century as Roiannum / Roianum (from a Gallo-Roman villa name *Roianum, personal name + Latin -anum). Unattested before 867; anachronistic under strict pre-867 attestation.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd–4th c. AD, Novioregum at Barzan)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman port of Novioregum (modern Barzan, ~20 km SE) was the classical estuary center before Royan (attested 11th c.).

b_saintes.first_mention_attestation: 1st century AD (Mediolanum Santonum; 4th c. Santonica Urbs / Urbs Santonorum)
b_saintes.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish-Roman Mediolanum Santonum ('central plain of the Santones', 1st c. AD), shortened from the 4th century to Urbs Santonorum / Santones, giving Saintes. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Ptolemy, and Roman inscriptions (1st–2nd c. AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Mediolanum Santonum ('central plain of the Santones') was shortened to Santones (> Saintes) by the 4th c.

b_armagnac.first_mention_attestation: c. 960 (Arminiaca / Comté d'Armagnac carved out of Fezensac in 960)

morphemes.translation: personal name Arminius or Germanic Hermann

b_armagnac.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Arminiacum (personal name Arminius or Germanic Hermann + suffix -acum). However, the county/polity of Armagnac was only created in 960 when William of Fezensac divided his county; unattested as a title before 867.

b_lectoure.first_mention_attestation: 1st–2nd century AD (Lactora; tribe of the Lactorates)

morphemes.translation: ancient oppidum of the Lactorates (possibly 'fortress of Laccos')

b_lectoure.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient city of Lactora (attested in the 1st–2nd c. AD, capital of the Lactorates), of Aquitanian or Celtiberian/Gaulish origin. Continuously inhabited and episcopal see; historical for 867.

b_lomagne.etymology_analysis: Gascon Lomanha (possibly from Latin ulmus 'elm' via *olmania 'elm grove', or medieval Leomania). Emerged as a viscounty in the late 10th century in the territory of the ancient Lactorates; unattested prior to 867.

b_fesensac.first_mention_attestation: 801–802 (Fidentiacus pagus; County of Fezensac erected under Charlemagne)
b_fesensac.etymology_analysis: From Latin Fidentiacus pagus (Latin personal name Fidentius + Gaulish suffix -acum), erected as a Carolingian county in 801/802. Clearly historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_pau.first_mention_attestation: 1154 (Castrum de Pado in the Charter of Barcelona)
b_pau.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1154 as Castrum de Pado, from Gascon pau (< Latin palus, 'stake/palisade'), referring to the palisaded castle built by the Viscounts of Béarn in the 11th–12th century. Clearly anachronistic for 867.

b_tursan.first_mention_attestation: c. 400 (Civitas Aturrensium in Notitia Galliarum; pagus Aturensis)
b_tursan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient hydronym Aturus (Adour River), attested via Civitas Aturrensium (c. 400) and pagus Aturensis. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_oloron.first_mention_attestation: 1st–2nd century AD (Iluro on a Roman milestone; c. 400 civitas Elloronensium)

natural_proper_name.name: Confluence of the Gaves d'Aspe and d'Ossau ('water-town')

b_oloron.etymology_analysis: Attested in Roman antiquity as Iluro (civitas Elloronensium c. 400), from Aquitanian/Proto-Basque ili ('town') + ur ('water'), referring to the confluence of the two gaves. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_tarbes.first_mention_attestation: c. 400 (Civitas Turba ubi castrum Bigorra; 6th c. Gregory of Tours: Talvam vicum)

morphemes.translation: ancient regional city name (distinct from the Tarbelli of Dax)

b_tarbes.etymology_analysis: First attested around 400 AD as Civitas Turba ubi castrum Bigorra (and 6th c. Talvam vicum), an ancient Aquitanian/pre-Roman city of Novempopulania. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_pardiac.first_mention_attestation: 1023 (County of Pardiac created by Bernard-Odon, son of Arnaud II of Astarac)
b_pardiac.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Pardiacum (Latin personal name Pardus + Gaulish suffix -acum). However, the County of Pardiac was only created in 1023 by partition of Astarac; unattested prior to 867.

b_bertrand_de_comminges.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (renamed after Bishop Bertrand of Comminges, d. 1123; ancient site was Lugdunum Convenarum, 72 BC)
b_bertrand_de_comminges.eponym_details: Named after Saint Bertrand of Comminges (c. 1050–1123, Bishop of Comminges from 1073–1123, lived well after 867)

morphemes.translation: gathered people (ancient tribe of the Convenae)

b_bertrand_de_comminges.etymology_analysis: Blatantly anachronistic for 867: named after Saint Bertrand, Bishop of Comminges (c. 1050–1123), who rebuilt the cathedral city after 1073. In 867 the site was known as Comminges (< Latin Convenae) or ancient Lugdunum Convenarum.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD (Strabo, Ptolemy: Lugdunum Convenarum); 585 AD (Gregory of Tours)
older_name_by_867.notes: Attested as Lugdunum Convenarum in antiquity and Comminges (Convenae) in the early Middle Ages before being renamed after Saint Bertrand (1050–1123).

b_saint_lizier.first_mention_attestation: 6th–7th century (episcopal city of Couserans renamed after Bishop Glycerius / Lizier, fl. 506)
b_saint_lizier.eponym_details: Named after Saint Lizier (Latin Glycerius / Licerius, Bishop of Couserans, attended Council of Agde in 506, pre-867)
b_saint_lizier.etymology_analysis: Named after Saint Lizier (Glycerius/Licerius), 6th-century Bishop of Couserans (fl. 506, pre-867), who succeeded the Roman Lugdunum Consoranorum. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Notitia Galliarum (c. 400 AD, Civitas Consorannorum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Lugdunum Consoranorum preceded Saint-Lizier (6th c.).

b_astarac.first_mention_attestation: 926 (County of Astarac created for Arnaud I; Latin Asteriacum)

morphemes.language: Aquitanian / Basque personal name (cf. Basque azter)

b_astarac.etymology_analysis: Medieval Latin Asteriacum / Asteirac, formed from the local Aquitanian/Gascon personal name Aster + suffix -acum. Although the root is pre-Roman/Gallo-Roman, the county/territory of Astarac was created in 926 and is unattested before 867.

b_muret.first_mention_attestation: 1076 (Murellum / Muret; castle and town on the Garonne and Louge)
b_muret.etymology_analysis: First attested in the late 11th century (1076, Murellum), from Occitan muret (< Latin murus + diminutive suffix, 'small wall/fortification'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_aurillac.first_mention_attestation: 899 (Aureliacus; abbey founded c. 885 by St. Gerald of Aurillac, born there c. 855)
b_aurillac.etymology_analysis: First attested in 899 as Aureliacus (Latin gentilicium Aurelius + Gaulish -acum, 'estate of Aurelius'). Already an active comital estate before 867 (Saint Gerald of Aurillac was born there c. 855). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_carlat.first_mention_attestation: 839 (Castrum quod vulgo Cartilatum dicitur, Annales Bertiniani)
b_carlat.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 839 in the Annales Bertiniani as Castrum quod vulgo Cartilatum dicitur. A Gaulish or Gallo-Roman formation in -ate (possibly on a root *kar- 'rock' or personal name Cartilus). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_murat.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1095 as Muratum, from Old Occitan murat (< Latin muratus, 'walled/fortified'), a medieval generic designation for a fortified settlement around the castle of Bonnevie. Anachronistic for 867.

b_clermont_sur_ailler.first_mention_attestation: 761 (Claromonte / Clarus Mons; earlier Roman Augustonemetum / Arvernis)

natural_proper_name.name: Clarus Mons ('bright/clear hill') + Allier River (in CK3 key)

b_clermont_sur_ailler.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish-Roman Augustonemetum and Arvernis; the fortress name Clarus Mons / Clarmont ('clear/bright hill', Latin clarus + mons) is attested from 761 (848 Clairmont). Historical for 867 (note: the '-Ferrand' union dates only to 1630, whereas CK3 uses 'Clermont-sur-Allier').

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Clârmunt-an-Aljêr).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy (2nd c. AD, Augustonemetum); 4th–6th c. (Arvernis)
older_name_by_867.notes: Called Augustonemetum in Roman antiquity and Arvernis in Late Antiquity before Clarus Mons (Clermont) became standard in 761.

b_la_tour.first_mention_attestation: 11th century (La Tor d'Auvèrnha; feudal house of La Tour)
b_la_tour.etymology_analysis: From Occitan La Tor ('the tower', Latin turris), referring to the medieval feudal keep of the House of La Tour d'Auvergne attested from the 11th century. No pre-867 attestation; anachronistic for 867.

b_mercaeur.first_mention_attestation: 10th century (Mercorium; lords of Mercœur attested from 938)
b_mercaeur.etymology_analysis: Occitan Mercuèr, from Latin Mercurius (likely referring to a Gallo-Roman sanctuary or estate dedicated to Mercury). However, the feudal lordship and settlement of Mercœur are first attested in the 10th century (938); unattested before 867.

b_montpensier.first_mention_attestation: 892 (Mons Pancarius / Mons Pancerius; medieval castle hill in Limagne)
b_montpensier.etymology_analysis: Attested from 892 as Mons Pancarius (later Montpansier), combining Latin mons ('hill') with the personal name Pancarius (or a slope-related modifier). First recorded after 867; anachronistic under strict 867 attestation.

b_thiers.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Castrum Thigernum in Gregory of Tours)
b_thiers.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 6th century by Gregory of Tours as Castrum Thigernum, derived from Gaulish *tigernos ('lord, master, chief'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

morphemes.translation: ford ('ford on both sides', or Germanic personal name Ansberht)

b_ambert.etymology_analysis: Possibly from Gaulish *Ambi-ritu ('ford' on the Dore) or a Germanic personal name (Ansberht / Ambert). However, the town is not attested in surviving charters until the 11th century; flagged anachronistic under strict 867 attestation.

b_le_puy.first_mention_attestation: 10th century (Podium Aniciense; earlier 6th–9th c. name was Anicium)
b_le_puy.etymology_analysis: From Latin podium > Occitan puèi / French puy ('peak, volcanic hill'). While the bishopric moved here in the 6th century, its pre-867 name was Anicium (Civitas Aniciensis); the name Podium ('Le Puy') only replaced Anicium in the 10th century. Anachronistic as a title name for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Gregory of Tours (6th c., Anicium)
older_name_by_867.notes: Anicium was the established pre-867 name of the episcopal city before Podium ('Le Puy') replaced it in the 10th c.

b_velay.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Vellavii in Caesar; Strabon: Velauni; Carolingian pagus Vellavensis)

morphemes.translation: the better ones / noble ones (Gaulish tribe of the Vellavii)

b_velay.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Gaulish tribe Vellavii (attested by Julius Caesar in 52 BC and Strabo), yielding the Carolingian pagus Vellavensis and modern Velay. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Hemmamarct — Disambiguated capital foundation: Chartered market borough established by Hemma
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_barcelona.first_mention_attestation: 3rd–2nd century BC (Iberian coins: Baŕkeno; Latin Barcino / Barcenona)
b_barcelona.etymology_analysis: Attested on 3rd–2nd c. BC Iberian coins as Baŕkeno (Greek Barkinṓn, Latin Barcino / Barcenona). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_sitges.etymology_analysis: From Catalan sitges ('underground grain silos'), first attested in 992 as the medieval castle of Sitges (succeeding ancient Roman Subur). Unattested before 867; anachronistic for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pomponius Mela (c. 43 AD) and Pliny the Elder (1st c. AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Subur is the classical predecessor of medieval Sitges (first attested 992).

b_manresa.first_mention_attestation: 889–890 (Minorisa; re-established by Wilfred the Hairy, though name Minorisa is Roman/pre-Roman)
b_manresa.etymology_analysis: From ancient Minorisa (attested in 889–890 upon Carolingian repopulation, preserving a pre-Roman/Roman toponym). Historically grounded by the late 9th century (note: current repo maps b_manresa to Cardona).

b_vic.first_mention_attestation: 879 (Vicus Ausonensis, rebuilt by Wilfred the Hairy; pre-867 name was Ausa / Ausona)
b_vic.etymology_analysis: From Latin vicus ('village/quarter', shortened from Vicus Ausonensis). In antiquity and up through the 8th–9th centuries the city was called Ausa / Ausona; it was only rebuilt and named Vicus (> Vic) in 879 by Count Wilfred the Hairy. Slightly anachronistic for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Iberian/Roman coinage & epigraphy (2nd c. BC, Ausa); Visigothic councils (516 AD, Ausona)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ausa / Ausona was the city's exact name until Count Wilfred the Hairy rebuilt it in 879 as Vicus Ausonensis (> Vic).

b_berga.first_mention_attestation: 195 BC (Livy: Castrum Bergium, capital of the Bergistani; 9th c. Berga)
b_berga.etymology_analysis: Linked to ancient Castrum Bergium mentioned by Livy (195 BC, capital of the Bargusii/Bergistani), from the root *berg- ('height/mountain'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

morphemes.translation: ancient city name (possibly 'at the river confluence')

b_girona.etymology_analysis: Founded by the Romans in the 1st century BC as Gerunda (incorporating an Iberian substrate name), continuously an episcopal and comital city through 867. Historical for 867.

b_loredo.first_mention_attestation: 966 (Lauredo, in a charter of Count Borrell II)
b_loredo.etymology_analysis: First attested in 966 as Lauredo (from Latin lauretum, 'laurel grove'). Although the site had Iberian ruins, the medieval settlement name Lauredo/Lloret is unattested before 867 (note: current repo maps b_loredo to Ullastret).

b_olot.first_mention_attestation: 872 (Olotis / Aulot, in a diploma of Charles the Bald)

morphemes.language: Pre-Roman / Iberian or Latin (ula / ala, disputed)
morphemes.translation: uncertain pre-Roman or early medieval toponym

b_olot.etymology_analysis: First attested in 872 (just five years after 867) as Olotis / Aulot in a diploma of Charles the Bald, confirming an existing pre-867 Carolingian settlement. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_lleida.first_mention_attestation: 3rd century BC (Iberian Iltirta; Roman Ilerda; Arabic Larida)

morphemes.translation: city of the Ilergetes (Roman Ilerda > Arabic Larida > Catalan Lleida)

b_lleida.etymology_analysis: Ancient Iberian capital Iltirta (3rd c. BC), Roman Ilerda, Andalusi Arabic Madīnat Larida (8th–9th c.), yielding Catalan Lleida. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Iberian coinage (Iltirta, 3rd–2nd c. BC) and Livy/Caesar (Ilerda)
older_name_by_867.notes: Iberian Iltirta and Roman Ilerda (Andalusi Larida) are direct ancestors of Lleida.

b_agramunt.first_mention_attestation: 1070 (conquered by Ermengol IV of Urgell; chartered 1163; Latin Acrimons)
b_agramunt.etymology_analysis: From Latin Acrimons / Agramunt ('sharp/steep hill'), first attested during the 11th-century Reconquista (1070, conquest by Ermengol IV of Urgell). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_prades.first_mention_attestation: 1090 (Andalusi fortress fortified in 1090; chartered 1159 by Ramon Berenguer IV)
b_prades.etymology_analysis: From Latin prata ('meadows', Catalan prades), referring to the mountain plateau of the Prades Mountains. First attested in 1090 as a fortified frontier castle; unattested prior to 867.

b_pallars_jussa.first_mention_attestation: 1010 (division of County of Pallars into Pallars Jussà and Pallars Sobirà; Pallars itself attested 800)
b_pallars_jussa.etymology_analysis: Combines the pre-Roman Pyrenean choronym Pallars (county founded 800) with Old Catalan jussà (< Latin deorsum, 'lower'). While 'Pallars' is pre-867, the subdivision 'Pallars Jussà' only arose in 1010 upon the testament of Count Sunyer I; anachronistic for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Carolingian County of Pallars (c. 800 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Unified Pallars existed from 800; the 'Jussà' ('Lower') division only dates to 1010.

b_pallars_sobira.first_mention_attestation: 1010 (division of County of Pallars into Pallars Sobirà and Pallars Jussà)
b_pallars_sobira.etymology_analysis: Combines pre-Roman Pallars (attested 800) with Old Catalan sobirà (< Latin superanus, 'upper'). Like Pallars Jussà, this political subdivision was only created in 1010; anachronistic for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Carolingian County of Pallars (c. 800 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Unified Pallars existed from 800; the 'Sobirà' ('Upper') division only dates to 1010.

b_vielha.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (Vetula / Vielha, capital of Val d'Aran)
b_vielha.etymology_analysis: From Aranese Occitan vielha (< Latin vetula, 'old [town]'), capital of the Val d'Aran. First attested in the 12th century; unattested prior to 867.

b_puigcerda.first_mention_attestation: 1178 (founded by King Alfonso II of Aragon on Mont Cerdà)
b_puigcerda.etymology_analysis: Founded ex nihilo in 1178 by King Alfonso II of Aragon on a hill (puig < Latin podium) in Cerdanya (Cerdà < ancient Ceretani) to replace Hix as capital. Blatantly anachronistic for 867 (note: current repo erroneously labels it an 'ancient hillfort').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Puigcerdà (ancient hillfort of the Cerretani) (in-game: Pûigserdâ)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from Llívia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Iulia Libica (1st c. BC; 673 Castrum Libyae); Hix attested 839 AD (Act of Consecration of Urgell Cathedral)
older_name_by_867.notes: Puigcerdà was founded ex nihilo in 1178 to replace Hix (attested 839) as capital of Cerdanya; Llívia / Iulia Libica was the ancient Roman capital.

b_llivia.first_mention_attestation: 1st century BC (Roman Julia Libica; 673 Castrum Libyae)

morphemes.translation: ancient capital of the Ceretani (Julia Libica)

b_llivia.etymology_analysis: Roman municipium Julia Libica (1st c. BC, succeeding an Iberian settlement of the Ceretani), attested as Castrum Libyae in 673. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Llívia / Iulia Libica (ancient Roman municipal capital of Cerretania) (in-game: Llîwje)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Roman capital Iulia Libica / Llívia.

b_perpignan.etymology_analysis: First attested in 927 as villa Perpiniani (Catalan Perpinyà), from a Gallo-Roman estate name *Perpennianum (Latin personal name Perpennius + -anum). While Roman in formation, the town only rose to prominence in the 10th century and is unattested before 867 (Ruscino was the ancient center).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy, Strabo, Pomponius Mela, Pliny (1st c. BC–1st c. AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ruscino (Château-Roussillon) was the attested pre-867 regional center of Roussillon before Perpignan (927) superseded it.

b_prades_rossello.first_mention_attestation: 843 (villa Prata, donated by Charles the Bald to Count Sunifred)

natural_proper_name.name: Meadows of the Conflent valley (Latin prata)

b_prades_rossello.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 843 as villa Prata in a charter of Charles the Bald to Count Sunifred of Urgell-Cerdanya, from Latin prata ('meadows'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_roses.first_mention_attestation: 5th–4th century BC (Greek colony of Rhode; Latin Rhoda; 9th c. Santa Maria de Roses)

morphemes.translation: Greek colony name (linked to Rhodes / rose)

b_roses.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Rhódē (Latin Rhoda, Catalan Roses), a Greek colony founded in the 5th–4th c. BC on the Bay of Roses and active as a monastic port in the 9th c. Historical for 867.

morphemes.translation: ancient city name (capital of Hispania Tarraconensis)

b_tarragona.etymology_analysis: Roman Tarraco (attested since 218 BC, capital of Hispania Tarraconensis), derived from a pre-Roman/Iberian toponym. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Iberian coinage (Kesse) and Polybius/Livy (218 BC, Tarraco)
older_name_by_867.notes: Iberian Kesse and Roman Tarraco precede modern Tarragona.

b_tortosa.first_mention_attestation: 1st century BC (Roman Dertosa; Andalusi Arabic Turtuixa)

morphemes.translation: ancient Ilercavonian/Roman city name on the Ebro

b_tortosa.etymology_analysis: Roman Dertosa (1st c. BC, in Ilercavonian territory), Andalusi Arabic Turtuixa (8th–9th c.), Catalan Tortosa. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (Ibera) and Roman coinage/Strabo (1st c. BC, Dertosa)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Dertosa (Andalusi Turtuixa) and probable Iberian predecessor Ibera precede Tortosa.

b_maials.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (Majals / Maials, post-Reconquista charter; Arabic/Romance origin)
b_maials.etymology_analysis: Although the hill has pre-Roman archaeological traces, the settlement name Maials is first documented only after the 12th-century Christian conquest of Lleida/Tortosa. Unattested prior to 867.

b_urgell.first_mention_attestation: 527 (Diocese of Urgell / Urgellum; 798 County of Urgell)
b_urgell.etymology_analysis: Attested since 527 as the episcopal see of Urgellum (and County of Urgell from c. 798), from a pre-Roman Pyrenean/Basque-like hydronymic root *ur- ('water'). Historical for 867.

b_seu_d_urgell.first_mention_attestation: 839 (Sedes Urgellensis, Cathedral Act of Consecration of 839)
b_seu_d_urgell.etymology_analysis: From Latin Sedes Urgellensis ('Episcopal See of Urgell'), attested as an episcopal city since 527 and in the 839 Act of Consecration. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_andorra.first_mention_attestation: 843 (copy of a charter of Charles the Bald; 903 Andorra)

morphemes.translation: ancient Pyrenean valley name (possibly linked to Andosini tribe or Basque *andur 'shrubland')

b_andorra.etymology_analysis: First attested in a copy of an 843 charter (and 903), of pre-Roman Pyrenean origin (possibly linked to the ancient Andosini tribe mentioned by Polybius). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_balaguer.first_mention_attestation: 9th century (Andalusi Madīnat Balaghī; pre-Roman *Balagaiu per Joan Coromines)

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name on the Segre

b_balaguer.etymology_analysis: Andalusi fortress city of Madīnat Balaghī (9th c.), preserving a pre-Roman Iberian toponym *Balagaiu consolidated before 800 (per Joan Coromines). Historical for 867 (note: current repo maps b_balaguer to Ordanyâ).

b_deols.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Dolensi / Dolensem Vicum in Gregory of Tours)

morphemes.translation: river bend, meadow, or low-lying place (Vicus Dolensis)

b_deols.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 6th century by Gregory of Tours as Dolensem Vicum (later Villa Dolis), from a Gaulish/pre-Celtic root *dol- (possibly referring to a river bend or low meadow on the Indre). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_chateauroux.first_mention_attestation: 10th century (Castrum Radulphi, castle built c. 937 by Raoul le Large, Prince of Déols)
b_chateauroux.eponym_details: Named after Raoul le Large (10th-century Prince of Déols, son of Ebbes le Noble, who built the castle c. 937, well after 867)
b_chateauroux.etymology_analysis: Latin Castrum Radulphi ('Castle of Raoul'), named after Raoul le Large, Prince of Déols, who built the fortress on the Indre in the 10th century (c. 937) after leaving Déols. Clearly anachronistic for 867 because it is named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Gallo-Roman vicus and Cluniac abbey of Déols / Vicus Dolensis on the Indre (in-game: Dôls)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 Gallo-Roman civitas restored over 937 Castrum Radulphi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Gregory of Tours (6th c., Dolensem Vicum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Before Raoul le Large built Châteauroux c. 937, the ancestral seat 2 km away was Déols (attested 6th c.).

b_la_haye.first_mention_attestation: c. 1155 (Haiam; later La Haye-en-Touraine, renamed Descartes in 1967)
b_la_haye.etymology_analysis: First attested c. 1155 as Haiam (Old French la haie < Frankish *hagja, 'hedge / enclosed woodland'). Unattested before 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_blois.first_mention_attestation: c. 584 (Blesenses / Blesensibus in Gregory of Tours; Merovingian coins Bleso castro)
b_blois.etymology_analysis: Attested c. 584 by Gregory of Tours (Blesenses) and on Merovingian coins (Bleso castro), from a Gaulish stem *Bles- (possibly related to *bleiso- 'wolf'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_contres.etymology_analysis: Derived from Late Latin contrata ('region/countryside') or possibly a reduced Gaulish *Condate, but the settlement of Contres in Loir-et-Cher has no pre-867 textual attestation; anachronistic for 867.

natural_proper_name.name: Morantin stream (Rivus Morentini, tributary of the Sauldre)

morphemes.translation: Morantin stream (or Latin personal name Morentinus)

b_romorantin.etymology_analysis: From Latin Rivus Morentini ('stream of Morantin', combining Old French ru < Latin rivus 'stream' + Morentinus, tributary of the Sauldre; folk-etymologized as Roma Minor). First attested in the 12th century; anachronistic as a barony title for 867.

b_issoudun.etymology_analysis: Attested in 984 as Uxellodunum (Gaulish uxello- 'high' + dunum 'fortress/citadel'), a classic pre-Roman Biturigan oppidum name whose linguistic coinage is unmistakably Gaulish/pre-867. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_valencay.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1144 as De Valentiaco, from Latin personal name Valentius + Gaulish suffix -acum ('estate of Valentius'). While the estate formation is Gallo-Roman in pattern, the settlement is unattested before 1144.

b_bourges.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Caesar: Avaricum; 4th c. Ammianus Marcellinus: Biturigae)

morphemes.translation: kings ('kings of the world', tribe of the Bituriges)

b_bourges.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Avaricum (52 BC), renamed Biturigae in the 4th century after the Gaulish tribe Bituriges (bitu- 'world' + -riges 'kings'), yielding Bourges. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (52 BC, Avaricum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Avaricum was the Gaulish-Roman name before Biturigae (> Bourges) replaced it in the 4th c.

b_tours.first_mention_attestation: 1st–2nd century AD (Caesarodunum; 4th c. Civitas Turonum / Turones)
b_tours.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Caesarodunum, replaced in the 4th century by the Gaulish tribal name Turones (> Tors > Tours). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy & Peutinger Table (1st–4th c. AD, Caesarodunum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Caesarodunum was the Roman name before Turones (> Tours) replaced it in the 4th c.

morphemes.translation: territorial suffix ('land of the Turones', Turonia)

b_tourraine.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin Turonia ('land of the Turones', tribal root Turon- + Latin -ia), yielding Touraine. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Emmerîchstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Emmerîch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_loches.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Lucca / vicus Loccae / Lucas castrum in Gregory of Tours)

morphemes.translation: bright/white place, or sacred grove (Latin lucus, disputed)

b_loches.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 6th century in Gregory of Tours as Lucca / vicus Loccae / Lucas castrum (later Leucas, Loiches). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_bellac.first_mention_attestation: 10th century (Bellacum; castle built by Boson I the Old, Count of La Marche, c. 950)
b_bellac.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Bellacum (personal name Bellus + -acum). However, the town and fortress of Bellac were founded in the mid-10th century by Boson I, Count of La Marche; unattested prior to 867.

b_la_tremouille.first_mention_attestation: 11th century (Tremolia / La Trimouille; feudal house attested c. 1040)
b_la_tremouille.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin tremula / *tremolia ('aspen grove'), seat of the House of La Trémoille attested from the mid-11th century. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_bourbon.first_mention_attestation: 3rd–4th century AD (Aquae Bormonis on Peutinger Table; 9th c. Borbonensis)

natural_proper_name.name: Thermal springs of the Gaulish god Borvo / Bormo ('bubbling/hot spring')

morphemes.translation: Gaulish healing god of hot/bubbling thermal springs

b_bourbon.etymology_analysis: Attested in Roman antiquity as Aquae Bormonis, named after the Gaulish thermal-spring deity Borvo / Bormo (*berw-, 'to boil/bubble'). Historical for 867 (note: the '-l'Archambault' suffix from the 10th–11th c. lords is not in the CK3 key b_bourbon).

natural_proper_name.name: Golden Valley (Latin Aurea Vallis, along the Cher)

b_orval.etymology_analysis: From Latin Aurea Vallis ('golden valley'), a high-medieval toponym attested from the late 11th century as a lordship on the Cher. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_montlucon.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 11th century as Monslucii ('hill of Lucius', Latin mons + personal name Lucius), developing around a medieval castle overlooking the Cher. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_boussac.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1095 as Cappella de Bociaco, from Gaulish personal name Boccius + suffix -acum ('estate of Boccius'). Although the root is Gaulish, the lordship and town are unattested before 1095.

b_saint_pourcain.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (monastery founded by Saint Porcianus / Pourçain, d. c. 532)
b_saint_pourcain.eponym_details: Named after Saint Porcianus / Pourçain (6th-century monk and abbot, d. c. 532, pre-867)
b_saint_pourcain.etymology_analysis: Named after Saint Porcianus (Pourçain), a 6th-century freedman and monk (d. c. 532) who founded the monastery around which the town grew. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_jaligny.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 11th century as Castrum Gallinici / Jaliniacum (Latin personal name Gallinius + Gaulish -acum, 'estate of Gallinius'). Unattested prior to 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Adalgodstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Adalgod
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_grandmont.first_mention_attestation: 1124 (Order of Grandmont moved from Muret to Grandmont after the death of Stephen of Muret in 1124)
b_grandmont.etymology_analysis: From Old French/Occitan grand mont ('great mountain'), founded as the motherhouse of the Order of Grandmont in 1124 by disciples of Saint Stephen of Muret (1046–1124). Clearly anachronistic for 867.

b_gueret.etymology_analysis: First attested c. 700 as Waractus (Occitan Garait) upon the foundation of its monastery, from Late Latin vervactum ('fallow/plowed land'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

morphemes.language: Latin personal name (Albucius) or Gaulish albuca
morphemes.translation: personal name Albucius or Gaulish 'clayey white earth'

b_aubusson.etymology_analysis: First attested in 936 as Albusiensis (1048 Albuzo), from Latin personal name Albucius + -onem (or Gaulish albuca 'clayey earth'). Unattested before 867; viscounty established in the 10th century.

b_auxerre.etymology_analysis: Attested in Roman antiquity as Autissiodorum / Autessiodorum (Gaulish stem + -duron 'fortified market/gate'), yielding Auxerre. Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_donzy.etymology_analysis: First attested c. 600 as Domiciacus, from Latin personal name Domitius + Gaulish suffix -acum ('estate of Domitius'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

morphemes.translation: windfall trees, fallen timber (Old French chaable > chablis)

b_chablis.etymology_analysis: First attested in 867 itself as Capleia (in pago Tornodorensi), from Late Latin *cataboleia (< Greek katabolē, Old French chablis 'windfall/felled trees'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_vezelay.first_mention_attestation: 868 (Virzelliacus; abbey founded c. 858–859 by Girart de Roussillon)

morphemes.translation: personal name Vertecillus (cf. Latin verticillus 'spindle whorl')

b_vezelay.etymology_analysis: Attested in 868 as Virzelliacus (abbey founded c. 858–859 by Girart de Roussillon), from Gallo-Roman *Vertecilliacum ('estate of Vertecillus'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Vizeliacum / Benedictine Abbey of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine at Vézelay (attested 858 AD) (in-game: Wêzelê)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic Pre-867 Historical Monastic Abbey (founded 858 AD).

morphemes.translation: wood, forest ('great forest', *maro-vidu-enno, per J. Lacroix)

b_morvan.etymology_analysis: Attested in Roman antiquity (Morvinnico) and c. 590 (Murvinnum), naming the forested massif of Burgundy (possibly Gaulish *maro-vidu-enno, 'great forest'). Historical for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Gallo-Roman Aballo / fortified caput of the Avalois on the Cousin (attested 843 AD) (in-game: Avalûn)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic Classical Antiquity / Pre-867 Gallo-Roman Civitas.

b_chalon.etymology_analysis: Attested by Julius Caesar in 52 BC as Cabillonum / Cavillonum (Gaulish caballos 'horse' or pre-Celtic *cab- 'height'), a major Aeduan port on the Saône. Historical for 867.

b_citeaux.first_mention_attestation: 1098 (Cistercium, abbey founded in 1098 by Robert of Molesme)
b_citeaux.etymology_analysis: Abbey founded in 1098 by Robert of Molesme in a marshy reedbed (Latin Cistercium, Old French cistel 'reeds'). Blatantly anachronistic as a barony title for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient pre-867 Vouge River reach in Burgundy (in-game: Citeaux)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1098 Cistercian mother abbey Cîteaux fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Vouge river hydronym.

natural_proper_name.name: Sacred spring of Belena (dedicated to the Gaulish god Belenos)

morphemes.translation: shining one (Gaulish god of springs and healing, giving the spring Belena)

b_beaune.etymology_analysis: Attested on Merovingian coins (BELENO CASTRO), in 664 (Pagus Balnensis), and in 861 (Belna), named after the sacred spring Belena dedicated to the Gaulish deity Belenos. Historical for 867.

b_autun.first_mention_attestation: c. 15 BC (Augustodunum, founded by Augustus; Tacitus 115 AD; 850 Augustodunensium)
b_autun.eponym_details: Named after Roman Emperor Augustus (63 BC–14 AD, pre-867)
b_autun.etymology_analysis: Founded under Augustus as Augustodunum ('fortress of Augustus', Latin Augustus + Gaulish -dunum), evolving via Agustidunum to Autun. Historical for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Augustodunum / Episcopal See of Autun (attested secondary variant of the Bishopric of Avalois) (in-game: Ostûn)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic Classical Antiquity / Pre-867 Roman Civitas.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (58 BC, Bibracte)
older_name_by_867.notes: Bibracte was the nearby Aeduan hillfort capital abandoned when Augustus founded Augustodunum (Autun) c. 15 BC.

b_dijon.first_mention_attestation: 6th century (Divione / Castrum Divionense in Gregory of Tours; 814 Castrum Divionense)
b_dijon.etymology_analysis: Attested from the Merovingian era (Divione, 814 Castrum Divionense, 836 Divion castrum), from Gaulish *Divio / *Divona ('sacred spring/place'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_gray.etymology_analysis: First attested in 910 as Gradiacus (Latin personal name Gratus + Gaulish -acum, 'estate of Gratus'). Although Gallo-Roman in pattern, the earliest surviving mention is 910 (post-867).

b_chaumont.first_mention_attestation: 1134 (Chalmunt; 1167 Calvus Mons; town founded in the 10th c.)

natural_proper_name.name: Bald rocky spur overlooking the Suize and Marne (Calvus Mons)

b_chaumont.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1134 as Chalmunt (1167 Calvus Mons, 'bald hill'), built on a treeless rocky spur in the 10th century. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_langres.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Andomatounon; 4th–6th c. Lingonas / Civitas Lingonum; 814 Lingonica civitas)

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Lingones ('the leapers / jumpers', *ling-)

b_langres.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Andematunnum (2nd c. AD), replaced in Late Antiquity by the ethnonym of the Gaulish Lingones (814 Lingonensium urbs), giving Langres. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy (2nd c. AD, Andomatounon) and Antonine Itinerary (Andemantunnum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Andematunnum was the Gaulish-Roman name before Lingones (> Langres) replaced it in Late Antiquity.

b_grand.first_mention_attestation: 4th century AD (Grannum; Merovingian Granno; earlier Andesina)

morphemes.translation: Celtic healing god Apollo Grannus (sanctuary of Grannus)

b_grand.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 4th century AD as Grannum (Merovingian Granno), derived from the major Gallo-Roman sanctuary of Apollo Grannus at Andesina. Historical for 867 (note: current repo maps b_grand to Poulanjî).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Peutinger Table (4th c. AD, Andesina)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman spa town Andesina preceded Grannum (Grand, named after Apollo Grannus).

b_champs.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1188 as Campi (Old French Chams > Champs, 'fields'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_macon.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Caesar: Matisco; 6th c. Gregory of Tours: Matiscone; 842 Nithard: Madasconis)

morphemes.translation: ancient Aeduan river port name (possibly *matu- 'good/bear' + suffix -isco)

b_macon.etymology_analysis: Attested by Julius Caesar in 52 BC as Matisco (842 Madasconis in Nithard), a major Aeduan/Burgundian city on the Saône. Historical for 867.

b_cluny.first_mention_attestation: 825 (Cluniacus; Carolingian villa donated in 910 to found Cluny Abbey)
b_cluny.etymology_analysis: First attested in 825 as the Carolingian villa Cluniacus (personal name Clunius + Gaulish -acum), predating the famous 910 Benedictine abbey foundation by 85 years. Historical for 867 as a settlement name (though the abbey itself is post-867).

b_semur_en_brionnais.first_mention_attestation: 879 (Senmurus; ruined pre-existing fortress, Latin senemurium / sine muro)
b_semur_en_brionnais.etymology_analysis: Attested in 879 as Senmurus (Latin senemurium 'old walls' or sine muro 'without wall'), referring to an older ruined hillfort in the Brionnais (territory of the ancient Branovii). Historically attested within 12 years of 867 as an existing site.

b_nevers.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Noviodunum (52 BC), renamed Nevirnum by the 3rd century (862 Nevernum) after the Nièvre River (*Nevera). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (52 BC, Noviodunum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Noviodunum ('new fortress') was the Gaulish name before Nevirnum (> Nevers) replaced it by the 3rd c.

b_moulins.etymology_analysis: First attested in 990 as villa Molinis (from Late Latin molinum, 'mill', referring to watermills on the Allier), becoming the Bourbon capital only in 1327. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

morphemes.translation: the waters (mineral spa suffix added in 1801)

b_pougues_les_eaux.etymology_analysis: Parish created in 1061, first attested as Poga in 1199, with the spa suffix '-les-Eaux' added only in 1801. Blatantly anachronistic for 867.

b_tonnerre.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 6th century (Ternodorense castrum) and 814 (Tornotrinse castrum), from Gaulish *turno ('hill') + *duro ('stronghold/market'). Historical for 867.

natural_proper_name.name: Hill barring the Brenne valley (Latin Mons + Gaulish *barro-)

b_montbard.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1065 as Castrum Barris Montis (1101 Mons Barrum), a pleonastic compound of Latin mons ('hill') + Gaulish *barro- ('summit/height'). Grew around an 11th-century fortress; unattested prior to 867.

b_chalons.first_mention_attestation: 3rd century AD (Durocatelauni; 4th c. Civitas Catuellaunorum; 834 Catalaunicum castrum)
b_chalons.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Durocatelauni (3rd c. AD), shortened in Late Antiquity to Catalauni (834 Catalaunicum castrum, 842 Cadhellonica), from the Gaulish tribal name Catalauni (*catu- 'battle' + *wellauno- 'chief'). Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd c. AD, Durocatelauni)
older_name_by_867.notes: Durocatelauni was shortened to Catalauni (> Châlons) in Late Antiquity.

b_saint_dizier.first_mention_attestation: 1190 (Sanctus Desiderius; in 854 and 875 the settlement was called Olonna, with a church of St. Desiderius)
b_saint_dizier.eponym_details: Named after Saint Desiderius of Langres (3rd–4th c. martyr, pre-867), though the town name itself was Olonna in 867
b_saint_dizier.etymology_analysis: In 854 and 875 the settlement was explicitly named Olonna (with a basilica consecrated to the 4th-c. martyr Saint Desiderius); the town only adopted the name Sanctus Desiderius (Saint-Dizier) in the late 12th century (1190). Anachronistic as the town name for 867 (Olonna is the 867 name).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Engeltraudszelle — Monastic cell and hermitage established by Engeltraud
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (1227 castle built by Guy II of Dampierre); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Engeltraud of House Châlons.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Charter of 854 AD (Olonna, cum ecclesia in honore sancti Desiderii)
older_name_by_867.notes: Explicitly attested as Olonna in 854 (and 875) before Sanctus Desiderius (> Saint-Dizier) replaced it in 1190.

b_vitry_en_perthois.etymology_analysis: Attested from the Merovingian period (6th c.) as Victoriacum castrum (Latin Victorius + Gaulish -acum), in the Carolingian pagus Pertensis (Perthois). Historical for 867.

b_provins.etymology_analysis: First attested in 802 as Pagus Provinensis (and 9th c. Castris Pruvinis), likely from the Latin personal name Probinus. Clearly historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_coulommiers.etymology_analysis: From Latin columbarium ('dovecote'), attested in the high Middle Ages as a fortified town of the Counts of Champagne. No verified pre-867 textual attestation; anachronistic under strict 867 attestation.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Klarastat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Klara
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_romilly.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1163 as Romeliacum (Gallo-Roman type *Romiliacum, Latin Romilius + Gaulish -acum). Although Gallo-Roman in pattern, the village is unattested before 1163.

b_meaux.first_mention_attestation: 1st century AD (Pliny: Meldi; 4th c. Meldorum civitas; 6th c. Meldensis civitas)
b_meaux.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Iatinum, replaced in Late Antiquity by the ethnonym of the Gaulish Meldi (attested since Pliny, 1st c. AD), evolving via Meldis to Meaux. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy (2nd c. AD, Iatinum) and Peutinger Table
older_name_by_867.notes: Iatinum was the original Gaulish-Roman name before Meldi (> Meaux) replaced it.

b_crecy.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Crisciacum (Latin/Gaulish personal name Criscius < crispus 'curly' + suffix -acum). While Gallo-Roman in type, Crécy-en-Brie is first attested in the late 11th century.

b_reims.first_mention_attestation: 57 BC (Caesar: Remi / Durocortorum; 4th c. Civitas Remorum)

morphemes.translation: the first ones / foremost (Gaulish tribe of the Remi)

b_reims.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Durocortorum ('circular stronghold'), renamed after the Gaulish tribe Remi (attested since Caesar, 57 BC) in Late Antiquity, giving Reims. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (57 BC, Durocortorum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Durocortorum was the Gaulish-Roman capital before Remi (> Reims) replaced it.

morphemes.language: Gaulish / Germanic (*sparna- 'thorn/hawthorn' or personal name Sparnus)

b_epernay.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 6th century as Sparnacus (from *sparna- 'thorn' or personal name Sparnus + Gaulish -acum), giving Épernay. Historical for 867.

b_chatillon.etymology_analysis: Built in the early 10th century by Hervé (nephew of Archbishop Hervé of Reims) and first attested in 940–949 as Castellionem ('small castle', Late Latin castellum + -ionem). Clearly anachronistic for 867.

b_chateau_thierry.first_mention_attestation: 923 (Castrum Theodorici in Flodoard's Annals; earlier Merovingian/Carolingian name was Otmus / pagus Otmensis)
b_chateau_thierry.eponym_details: Tradition links it to Merovingian king Theuderic IV (pre-867), or a 9th–10th c. lord Theuderic; however, the name Castrum Theodorici is unattested before 923

morphemes.translation: ruler of the people (personal name Thierry)

b_chateau_thierry.etymology_analysis: First attested in 923 by Flodoard as Castrum Theodorici ('Castle of Thierry'). In the Merovingian and Carolingian periods before 923 the town/district was called Otmus (pagus Otmensis). Anachronistic as a title name for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Folkmarsburch — Disambiguated capital foundation: Self-eponymous fortress founded by Folkmar (['ambitious'])
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Merovingian coinage (Otm[us]) and Carolingian texts (pagus Otmensis)
older_name_by_867.notes: Merovingian coins and Carolingian texts attest Otmus / pagus Otmensis prior to Flodoard's 923 mention of Castrum Theodorici.

b_rethel.first_mention_attestation: 974 (Retest / County of Rethel; earlier 7th c. Villa Regitestis in Abbey of Saint-Remi records)
b_rethel.etymology_analysis: Attested as Villa Regitestis in early medieval records of the Abbey of Saint-Remi (later Retest in 974, evolving to Rethel). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_grandpre.first_mention_attestation: 11th century (Grandis Pratus; Counts of Grandpré attested from c. 1008)

natural_proper_name.name: Great meadow along the Aire River (Latin Grandis Pratus)

b_grandpre.etymology_analysis: From Old French/Latin Grandis Pratus ('great meadow'), seat of the Counts of Grandpré attested from the early 11th century (c. 1008). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_mezieres.first_mention_attestation: 899 (Maceriae; fortified town built on the Meuse meander in the late 9th–10th c.)
b_mezieres.etymology_analysis: From Latin maceriae ('ruins, stone enclosure walls'), first attested in 899 when a fortress was built on the Meuse meander (Charleville was founded separately in 1606). Unattested prior to 867.

b_romigny.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 840–877 as Rominiacus (Latin personal name Rominius + Gaulish suffix -acum, 'estate of Rominius'). Historical for 867; not named after a post-867 person.

b_sens.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Caesar: Agedincum; c. 350 Ammianus Marcellinus: Senones; 519 Senonum civitas)

morphemes.translation: the elders / ancient ones (Gaulish tribe of the Senones)

b_sens.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Agedincum (52 BC), replaced by the tribal name Senones (from Gaulish *seno- 'old/elder') by c. 350 AD, giving Sens. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (52 BC, Agedincum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Agedincum was the Gaulish-Roman name before Senones (> Sens) replaced it around 350 AD.

b_nogent.first_mention_attestation: 859 (villa of Nogent in the pagus of Morvois, refuge of monks of Saint-Denis; earlier Novigentum)
b_nogent.etymology_analysis: From Gaulish *Novigentum (novio- 'new' + -entum 'settlement'), explicitly attested in 859 when the monks of Saint-Denis took refuge in their villa at Nogent. Historical for 867.

b_aube.first_mention_attestation: Early Middle Ages (Latin Albis; 877 Alba, river Aube)

morphemes.translation: white (referring to the chalky white waters/bed of the Aube River)

b_aube.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Aube River (Latin Albis, 877 Alba), from the pre-Celtic/Latin hydronymic root *alb- ('white', referencing the chalk plains of Champagne). Historical for 867.

b_bar_sur_seine.first_mention_attestation: 9th century (Barrum / Bar-sur-Seine, comital stronghold in the pagus Latiscensis)

natural_proper_name.name: Fortified hilltop (*barro-) on the Seine River (Sequana)

b_bar_sur_seine.etymology_analysis: From Gaulish *barro- ('summit/hilltop') on the Seine River (Sequana), attested from the late 9th century as a Carolingian comital seat in the Lassois. Historical for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Bar-an-der-Sêne (ancient comital seat on the Seine) regularized to Franconian river-affix (in-game: Bar-Sur-Seine)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: French river preposition -sur- regularized to Franconian -an-der-.

b_troyes.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD (Ptolemy: Augustobona; 4th c. Civitas Tricassium / Tricasses)

morphemes.translation: curls / helmets / tribes ('tribe of the Tricasses')

b_troyes.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Augustobona (c. 150 AD), replaced in Late Antiquity by the Gaulish tribal name Tricasses (tri- 'three' + -casses), yielding Troyes. Historical for 867.
