b_quercy.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Caesar: Cadurci; Late Latin pagus Cadurcinus)

morphemes.translation: belonging to ('territory of the Cadurci', Cadurcinus > Quercy)

b_quercy.etymology_analysis: From Latin pagus Cadurcinus ('territory of the Cadurci', Gaulish tribe attested since Caesar, 52 BC), evolving via Caorcin to Quercy. Historical for 867.

b_montauban.first_mention_attestation: 1144 (Mons Albanus, bastide founded in 1144 by Count Alfonso Jordan of Toulouse)

natural_proper_name.name: White/willow hill (Latin Mons Albanus / Occitan Montalban)

b_montauban.etymology_analysis: Founded ex nihilo in 1144 by Count Alfonso Jordan of Toulouse as one of the earliest planned bastides (Latin Mons Albanus, 'white/willow hill'). Blatantly anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Violantesburch — Self-eponymous fortress founded by Violante (['greedy'])
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (1144 bastide founded by Alfonso Jordan); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Violante under Toponym-First foundation (disqualifying circular in-game house).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Carolingian foundation of the Abbey of Montauriol / Saint-Martin (c. 820–830 under Louis the Pious)
older_name_by_867.notes: Before the 1144 bastide of Montauban, the pre-867 abbey and settlement on the site was Montauriol (founded c. 820–830).

b_cahors.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Ptolemy: Divona; 4th c. Civitas Cadurcorum)

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Cadurci (replacing Divona 'sacred spring')

b_cahors.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Divona ('divine spring'), replaced in Late Antiquity by Civitas Cadurcorum (after the Gaulish Cadurci), evolving into Cahors. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy (2nd c. AD, Deouona / Divona)
older_name_by_867.notes: Divona ('divine spring') was the original Gaulish name before Cadurci (> Cahors) replaced it.

b_figeac.first_mention_attestation: 838 (Figiacus, in a diploma of Pepin I of Aquitaine)
b_figeac.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 838 as Figiacus in a diploma of Pepin I of Aquitaine (Gallo-Roman personal name + -acum). Historical for 867.

b_rodez.first_mention_attestation: 1st century BC (Segodunum; 4th c. Civitas Rutenorum / Rutenis)

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Ruteni (replacing Segodunum 'strong fortress')

b_rodez.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Segodunum ('victory/strong fortress'), renamed Civitas Rutenorum / Rutenis in Late Antiquity after the Gaulish Ruteni, giving Rodez. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy and Peutinger Table (2nd–4th c. AD, Segodunum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Segodunum ('strong/victory fortress') preceded Rutenis (> Rodez).

b_la_salle.etymology_analysis: From Occitan sala (< Germanic *sal-, 'lordly hall/manor', historically Salles-Comtaux), attested from the 12th century. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_marvejols.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1060 as Marojol / Marojulia, from the unmistakable pre-Roman Gaulish compound *Maro-ialo ('great clearing'). Linguistically pre-867, though first attested in surviving charters in 1060.

natural_proper_name.name: Rocky cliff / paved stone road (Occitan peirada < Latin petrata)

b_la_peyrade.etymology_analysis: From Occitan la peirada (< Latin petrata, 'stony place / paved road'). Unattested as a settlement prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_toulouse.first_mention_attestation: 2nd–1st century BC (Posidonius, Strabo: Tolossa; Cicero, Caesar: Tolosa)

morphemes.translation: ancient city name of the Volcae Tectosages

b_toulouse.etymology_analysis: Attested since the 2nd–1st century BC as Tolosa (capital of the Volcae Tectosages, later Visigothic and Carolingian capital), of pre-Indo-European/Aquitanian origin. Historical for 867.

b_pamiers.first_mention_attestation: 1111 (Castrum Appamiae, named after Apamea in Syria by Count Roger II of Foix after the First Crusade; earlier site was Frédélas)
b_pamiers.eponym_details: Named in 1111 by Count Roger II of Foix (post-867 crusader) after Apamea in Syria

morphemes.translation: Apamea in Syria (transferred Crusader castle name)

b_pamiers.etymology_analysis: Named Castrum Appamiae (> Pamiers) in 1111 by Count Roger II of Foix returning from the First Crusade, in memory of Apamea in Syria (replacing the older Carolingian name Frédélas / Abbey of Saint-Antonin). Blatantly anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient 9th-century Benedictine abbey of Saint-Antonin on the Ariège (in-game: Pamiers)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1111 crusader fortress of Roger II of Foix fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to pre-867 monastic foundation.

morphemes.language: Occitan / Medieval Latin (personal name Cerrucius, folk-etymologized as 'Saracen')
morphemes.translation: castle of Cerrucius (later reinterpreted as 'Saracen castle')

b_castelsarrasin.etymology_analysis: First attested in 961 as Castrum Cerrucium (and 1156 Castro Sarreceno, Occitan castèl 'castle' + personal name Cerrucius, later reshaped by folk etymology to 'Sarrasin'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient 659 AD Benedictine Abbey of Moissac on the Tarn (in-game: Moissac)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 Benedictine Abbey restored over 961 Castel Sarracenum.

b_beaumont_sur_leze.first_mention_attestation: 13th century (Bellus Mons / Beaumont-sur-Lèze, medieval fortified village on the Lèze)

natural_proper_name.name: Lèze River (combined with medieval Bellus Mons 'fair hill')

b_beaumont_sur_leze.etymology_analysis: From Occitan/French Belmunt / Beaumont ('fair hill') on the Lèze River, a high-medieval bastide/fortified village unattested prior to 867. Anachronistic for 867.

b_amiens.first_mention_attestation: 57 BC (Caesar: Samarobriva / Ambiani; 4th c. Civitas Ambianorum)

morphemes.translation: people on both sides [of the Somme] (replacing Samarobriva)

b_amiens.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Samarobriva ('bridge on the Somme'), replaced in the 4th century by the tribal name Ambiani (attested since Caesar, 57 BC), yielding Amiens. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (57 BC, Samarobriva)
older_name_by_867.notes: Samarobriva ('bridge on the Somme') was the Gaulish-Roman name before Ambiani (> Amiens) replaced it.

b_corbie.first_mention_attestation: 662 (Corbie Abbey founded by Queen Balthild; 841 Corbiense monasterium; 877 Corbeia)

natural_proper_name.name: Corbiea amnis (ancient name of the Ancre River, or Latin Corvidius)

morphemes.language: Pre-Roman hydronym or Latin personal name (Corvidius < corvus 'raven')
morphemes.translation: Ancre River (Corbiea amnis) or estate of Corvidius

b_corbie.etymology_analysis: Famous royal Merovingian abbey founded in 662 (841 Corbiense monasterium, 877 Corbeia), named either after the local stream (Corbiea amnis) or Gallo-Roman Corvidius. Clearly historical for 867.

b_peronne.first_mention_attestation: 585 (Perrunas in Venantius Fortunatus's Life of Saint Radegund)
b_peronne.etymology_analysis: First attested in 585 by Venantius Fortunatus as Perrunas, from a Gaulish stem + hydronymic suffix -onna ('spring'). Historical for 867.

b_beaumont.first_mention_attestation: 1110 (Bellimontis; 1170 Bellus mons; medieval 'Beaumont' toponyms do not appear before the 10th c.)

natural_proper_name.name: Fair hill overlooking the Oise (Latin Bellus Mons)

b_beaumont.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1110 as Bellimontis (Old French Biaumont < Latin Bellus Mons, 'fair hill'); scholarly toponymy confirms no 'Beaumont' place-name is attested before the 10th century. Clearly anachronistic for 867.

b_mantes.first_mention_attestation: 9th century (Medanta / Medonta; from hydronym Medante fluminis)

natural_proper_name.name: Medante flumen (local stream/channel of the Seine)

b_mantes.etymology_analysis: Attested from the Carolingian era as Medanta / Medonta, transferred from the hydronym Medante fluminis. Historical for 867.

b_beauvais.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (Caesaromagus Bellovacorum; 5th c. Bellovacis; 583 Belloaca urbs; 845 Bellovacus)

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Bellovaci (replacing Caesaromagus)

b_beauvais.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Caesaromagus (2nd c. AD), renamed Bellovacis by the 5th century (845 Bellovacus) after the Belgic Gaulish tribe Bellovaci, giving Beauvais. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (57 BC, Bratuspantium); Ptolemy (2nd c. AD, Caesaromagus)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Caesaromagus preceded Bellovacis (> Beauvais).

b_montfort.first_mention_attestation: 999 (Mons Fortis; fortress built at the end of the 10th c. by Robert II / William of Hainaut)
b_montfort.eponym_details: Note: modern '-l'Amaury' honors Amaury I of Montfort (11th c., post-867), while the bare key b_montfort reflects the 999 castle Mons Fortis
b_montfort.etymology_analysis: First attested in 999 as Mons Fortis ('strong hill'), fortified at the end of the 10th century to defend the royal domain of Île-de-France. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: March fortress citadel of House Montfort (in-game: Montfort)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: c. 990 fortress of Amaury de Montfort fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved via Option C march stronghold.

b_melun.first_mention_attestation: 52 BC (Caesar: Metiosedum / Meteglum; 538 Mecledonensem; Merovingian Meclidone)

morphemes.translation: uncertain Gaulish root (possibly 'harvester' or personal name)

b_melun.etymology_analysis: Attested by Julius Caesar in 52 BC as an oppidum of the Senones on an island in the Seine (Metiosedum / Metlosedum, 538 Mecledonensem), evolving into Melun. Historical for 867.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_bray.first_mention_attestation: 958 (Villa que dicitur Brayacus / Braiacus, in pago Senonico)

natural_proper_name.name: Muddy marsh / river flats along the Seine (Gaulish *bracu)

b_bray.etymology_analysis: First attested in 958 as Brayacus / Braiacus (from Gaulish *bracu 'mud/marsh' + -acum). Although Gaulish in root, the settlement is unattested prior to 958.

morphemes.translation: sacred place suffix (Nemausus > Nemours, cognate with Nîmes)

b_nemours.etymology_analysis: Attested c. 843 as Nemausus (Gaulish *nem- 'sacred sanctuary' + -ausus, identical to the ancient name of Nîmes), evolving into Nemours. Historical for 867.

b_montereau.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th century (Monasteriolum; 1176 Musterolium; ancient Gaulish/Roman name was Condate)
b_montereau.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Condate ('confluence' of the Seine and Yonne); the medieval name Monasteriolum (> Montereau, 'small monastery') is first attested in the early 12th century. Anachronistic as a title name for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antonine Itinerary and Peutinger Table (3rd–4th c. AD, Condate)
older_name_by_867.notes: Condate ('confluence' of the Seine and Yonne) was the attested antique name before medieval Monasteriolum (> Montereau) appeared in the 12th c.

natural_proper_name.name: Clear/bright hill in Beauvaisis (Latin Clarus Mons)

b_clermont.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1023 (Baldinus de Clarimonte, Latin Clarus Mons 'clear hill'), becoming the seat of the Counts of Clermont-en-Beauvaisis in the 11th century. Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Bowês — Historical Option A seat of c_clermont

b_noyon.first_mention_attestation: 3rd century AD (Noviomagus; 6th c. Novionum; bishopric transferred here in 531)

morphemes.translation: plain, field, market ('new market', Noviomagus > Noyon)

b_noyon.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 3rd century as Gaulish Noviomagus ('new market'), episcopal seat since 531 and coronation site of Charlemagne (768). Historical for 867.

b_saint_quentin.first_mention_attestation: 7th century (basilica of Saint-Quentin rebuilt by St. Eligius in 641; earlier Roman Augusta Viromanduorum)
b_saint_quentin.eponym_details: Named after Saint Quentin (Latin Quintinus, 3rd-century Christian martyr, pre-867)
b_saint_quentin.etymology_analysis: Originally Roman Augusta Viromanduorum, renamed after the 3rd-century martyr Saint Quentin (pre-867), whose major pilgrimage basilica and town flourished from the 7th–9th centuries. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy & Antonine Itinerary (2nd–3rd c. AD, Augusta Viromanduorum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Augusta Viromanduorum was the Roman city name before Saint-Quentin replaced it in the 7th c.

morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Parisii (replacing Lutetia)

b_paris.etymology_analysis: Originally Gaulish Lutetia (53 BC), renamed Parisios by c. 400 after the Gaulish tribe Parisii. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Julius Caesar (53 BC, Lutetia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Lutetia was the Gaulish-Roman name before Parisios (> Paris) replaced it by c. 400.

b_saint_denis.first_mention_attestation: 5th–7th century (basilica of Saint Denis built c. 475 and royal abbey expanded by Dagobert I c. 630; earlier Catulliacus)
b_saint_denis.eponym_details: Named after Saint Denis / Dionysius (3rd-century first Bishop of Paris and martyr, pre-867)
b_saint_denis.etymology_analysis: Royal Merovingian and Carolingian abbey town built over the tomb of 3rd-century martyr Saint Denis (pre-867), superseding Gallo-Roman Catulliacus well before 867. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Vita Sanctae Genovefae (c. 520 AD, vicus Catolacus)
older_name_by_867.notes: Catulliacus was the Gallo-Roman settlement name prior to the basilica and abbey town of Saint-Denis.

b_montreuil.first_mention_attestation: 722 (Monasteriola in a diploma of Merovingian king Theuderic IV, though authenticity is debated; securely attested 12th c.)
b_montreuil.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin monasteriolum ('small monastery'), attributed to a 722 Merovingian diploma of Theuderic IV (though scholars note the document may be an 11th-c. forgery). Tentatively historical for 867 (note the authenticity caveat).

b_versailles.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1038 as Versalliis (Old French versail, 'cleared/plowed land', from Latin versare). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Walramsburch — Self-eponymous fortress founded by Walram (['fickle'])
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 foundation lacking pre-867 attestation under Burden of Proof on Antiquity (1038 medieval village); resolved via Option C based on save ruler Walram of House Carenwall.

b_montlhery.first_mention_attestation: 768 (Mons Ætricus; 798 Aetricus mons; c. 1061 de monte Leterico)
b_montlhery.eponym_details: Named after a pre-867 Frankish landholder named Leotheric / Liuderich (attested by 768)
b_montlhery.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 768 as Mons Ætricus and 798 as Aetricus mons (corrupted Latinization of Mons Leotherici, 'hill of Leotheric'). Historical for 867.

b_etampes.etymology_analysis: Attested in 587 (pago Stampensi) and 642–658 (Stampas) as a Merovingian and Carolingian royal domain. Historical for 867.

morphemes.language: Gaulish ethnonym (*selvano- 'possession/herd', later influenced by Latin silva 'forest')
morphemes.translation: Gaulish tribe of the Silvanectes (replacing Augustomagus)

b_senlis.etymology_analysis: Attested since 48 AD as civitas Sulbanectium / Augustomagus Silvanectum (from the Gaulish tribe Silvanectes), evolving into Senlis. Historical for 867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder & Ptolemy (1st–2nd c. AD, Augustomagus Silvanectum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Augustomagus Silvanectum was shortened to Silvanectes (> Senlis) in Late Antiquity.

b_crepy.first_mention_attestation: Early 11th century (Crispeium in Valesia / Crispiacus; capital of County of Valois from late 10th c.)
b_crepy.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Crispiacum (Latin Crispius + Gaulish -acum), becoming the fortified seat of the Counts of Valois in the late 10th–early 11th century. Unattested prior to 867.

b_coucy.first_mention_attestation: 530 (Codiciacum, donated to the Diocese of Reims; 1116 castellum Cociaci)
b_coucy.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested in 530 as Codiciacum (donated by Clovis/Saint Remigius to the Church of Reims), from Gallo-Roman personal name Codicius + -acum. Historical for 867 (note: the castle was added in the 10th c., so the repo's 'Koutzîveste' is anachronistic as a fortress name, whereas Coucy itself is pre-867).

current_repo_state.b_origin: March fortress citadel of Coucy (in-game: Coucy)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: c. 920 fortress of Archbishop Herve fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved via Option C march stronghold.

b_marle.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1112 as Castellum Marna (later Marla), from Gallo-Roman *margila (< Gaulish marga, 'marl'). Unattested prior to 867; anachronistic for 867.

b_roucy.first_mention_attestation: c. 948 (Rauciacum / Rosci, fortress built by Ragenold, first Count of Roucy, in 948)
b_roucy.etymology_analysis: From Gallo-Roman *Rosciacum (personal name Roscius + -acum), first attested in the mid-10th century (c. 948) when Ragenold built the fortress on the hill above the Aisne. Unattested prior to 867.

b_laon.etymology_analysis: Attested in 549 (and 632 Leudunum, 680 Laodunum), from Gaulish *Lugudunum ('citadel of the god Lugus'), an ancient bishopric and key Carolingian royal fortress. Historical for 867.
